summary: Defines managed objects describing the behavior of an SNMP entity itself, as a Management Information Base module. It covers system-level information and SNMP statistics so a manager can query how an agent is doing. It replaces RFC 1907, the MIB for SNMPv2.

eli5.summary: Every network gadget keeps a little notebook about itself. This note lists what goes in the notebook that describes the network-management software, so a manager can read it.

subtitle: The standard MIB module describing an SNMP entity itself: its identity, the MIB modules it supports, its message counters and its core notifications.

tldr.problem: A manager needs a common set of objects that every SNMP entity exposes, so it can learn what a device is, how long it has run and how its SNMP service is behaving.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SNMPv2-MIB module in SMIv2: a system group, an SNMP group of counters, notification objects, the cold start, warm start and authentication failure traps, and a set-coordination lock.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 62) that obsoletes RFC 1907 and has not been obsoleted. Many older RFC 1213 counters are marked obsolete in it.

today: RFC 3418 is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and is not obsoleted or updated by any later RFC listed for it. It obsoletes RFC 1907, and its objects such as sysUpTime and snmpTrapOID are used by the protocol operations in RFC 3416.

sections.title: What This MIB Module Is For
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB), usually using SNMP. The objects are written with the Structure of Management Information, and this module follows SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579, RFC 2580).

The goal is to define managed objects that describe the behavior of an SNMP entity, as defined by the SNMP architecture in RFC 3411. The module is named SNMPv2-MIB, and the RFC uses the RFC 2119 key words such as MUST and SHOULD.
sections.eli5: This is the fact sheet template for the part of a device that talks network management.

sections.title: The System Group
sections.content:
The system group sits at { mib-2 1 } and holds objects common to all managed systems.

  • sysDescr: a text description of the entity, up to 255 characters, which should include the hardware type, operating system and networking software.
  • sysObjectID: the vendor's authoritative identifier, allocated under the enterprises subtree 1.3.6.1.4.1.
  • sysUpTime: time since the network management portion was last re-initialized, in hundredths of a second.
  • sysContact, sysName and sysLocation: read-write text values. By convention sysName is the node's fully-qualified domain name.
  • sysServices: a number from 0 to 127 that encodes which protocol layers the node performs services for.

For sysServices, 2 raised to (L - 1) is added to the sum for each layer L from 1 through 7 the node serves. The RFC's examples are a routing-only node with a value of 4 and an application host with a value of 72.
sections.eli5: The device writes down its own name, what kind of box it is, who to call, where it sits and how long it has been awake.

sections.title: Describing Supported MIB Modules
sections.content:
Some devices can add or remove support for MIB modules while running. To describe this, the system group includes sysORTable, a conceptual table listing the capabilities of the local command responder with respect to MIB modules. The number of rows varies with the entity's configuration.

Each row, indexed by sysORIndex (1 to 2147483647), has sysORID (an authoritative identification of a capabilities statement), sysORDescr (a text description) and sysORUpTime (the value of sysUpTime when the row was last instantiated). The scalar sysORLastChange records the sysUpTime value at the most recent change to any sysORID instance.
sections.eli5: It is a list of the extra topics the device knows how to talk about, with a note of when the list last changed.

sections.title: SNMP Statistics and Control
sections.content:
The snmp group at { mib-2 11 } provides basic instrumentation and control. All are Counter32 values except where noted:

  • snmpInPkts: messages delivered to the entity from the transport service.
  • snmpInBadVersions: messages for an unsupported SNMP version.
  • snmpInASNParseErrs: ASN.1 or BER errors found when decoding messages.
  • snmpInBadCommunityNames and snmpInBadCommunityUses: community-based messages with an unknown community name, or with an operation the community was not allowed.
  • snmpSilentDrops: confirmed-class PDUs dropped because even an empty-bindings reply was too large. This is the counter the protocol operations RFC (RFC 3416) refers to.
  • snmpProxyDrops: confirmed-class PDUs dropped because forwarding to a proxy target failed in a way that left no response to return.

snmpEnableAuthenTraps is read-write, with values enabled(1) and disabled(2). It overrides other configuration and so can switch off all authenticationFailure traps. The RFC strongly recommends keeping it in non-volatile memory.

Many other counters from RFC 1213 (RFC 1213), such as snmpOutPkts and snmpInGetRequests, remain defined here but with status obsolete, grouped in snmpObsoleteGroup.
sections.eli5: The device keeps tally marks: how many messages came in, how many were garbled, and how many it had to throw away because the answer would not fit.

sections.title: Notifications and Set Coordination
sections.content:
Two objects support notifications. snmpTrapOID identifies the notification being sent and is the second binding in every SNMPv2-Trap-PDU and InformRequest-PDU. snmpTrapEnterprise identifies the enterprise tied to a trap, and appears as the last binding when a proxy maps an older Trap-PDU into an SNMPv2 one.

The module defines well-known traps. coldStart means the entity is reinitializing and its configuration may have changed. warmStart means it is reinitializing with its configuration unaltered. authenticationFailure means a protocol message that was not properly authenticated was received. Whether that last trap is generated is controlled by snmpEnableAuthenTraps. The linkDown and linkUp traps are defined in RFC 2863 (RFC 2863).

snmpSetSerialNo is an advisory lock that lets cooperating command generators coordinate their use of the set operation. It is coarse-grained, and finer-grained locks may be defined inside other MIB groups.
sections.eli5: The device can shout "I just restarted!" or "someone tried to get in without the right password!" It also has a sign-in sheet so two managers do not change things at the same time.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content:
The module groups its objects into units of conformance. systemGroup holds the system objects, snmpGroup the core SNMP counters and control, snmpCommunityGroup the two community counters, snmpSetGroup the set lock, and snmpBasicNotificationsGroup the coldStart and authenticationFailure notifications.

The current compliance statement, snmpBasicComplianceRev2, makes snmpGroup, snmpSetGroup, systemGroup and snmpBasicNotificationsGroup mandatory. The community group is mandatory for entities that support community-based authentication. The warm start group is mandatory for an entity that supports command responders and can reinitialize with its configuration unaltered. The older snmpBasicCompliance is deprecated and replaced by Rev2.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist saying which parts of the fact sheet every device must fill in and which are only needed in special cases.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Several objects here have a MAX-ACCESS of read-write and may be sensitive or vulnerable in some environments. Supporting SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations.

The RFC says that SNMPv1 alone is not secure, and that even on a secure network (for example with IPSec) nothing controls who may GET or SET these objects. It recommends the SNMPv3 security features: the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). Operators must configure access so that only principals with legitimate rights can read or change these objects.
sections.eli5: Some of the fact sheet can be edited. If anyone can edit it, they could cause trouble, so you must make sure only the right people can.
